items.body: “It personally feels like the discovery of a new path awaiting exploration,” writes Marco Paltrinieri about Otto Studi (Eight Studies). With this album, the Italian artist appears to abandon any narrative drive: vocals are gone, and any intrusion of fictional or literary framing—once suggested through evocative titles or references to Joseph Conrad in earlier works such as Ripari Minimi—is now neutralised. Instead, we are given only locations scattered across the Cévennes region in France—the album was recorded in Chalap in mid-July 2025—their geographic coordinates functioning as bare data, a record of time and place. This stripped-back, empirical approach restricts the palette to electric guitar and a handful of pedals. Notes are no longer permitted to bloom into the resonant microcosms of ambience that once allowed musique concrète textures to develop; they are held closer, more contained, and resistant to narrative suggestion. With Otto Studi, Paltrinieri turns toward the interstices of sound, encouraging the pedals to act as subtle perturbing forces, with fuzz blurring edges rather than overwhelming them. Sonic droplets fall without ripples, suspended within an aural canvas that feels bracketed by silence. Yet despite their brevity, these pieces do not register as fragments. Each study carries the weight of intention, unfolding as a fully realised sketch rather than a tentative note. Paltrinieri proves attentive to small gestures, to the spaces between tones, and to the quiet discipline of reduction. What emerges is a work of restraint and focus, where absence becomes a compositional tool and listening itself is gently recalibrated. To guide us through the making of the album, we reached out to Marco Paltrinieri via email. photo by Alan Chies Your previous works such as The Weaver, L’Altra Parte, and Ripari Minimi often combined sound with narrative, spoken text, literature, and speculative reflection. With Otto Studi, all of that seems to disappear, leaving only electric guitar, pedals, and the names of places in the Cévennes. What led you toward this radical reduction, and did it feel like a liberation or a constraint? When I recorded The Weaver and L’Altra Parte I was coming back to music after a 12 year hiatus. It was also the first time ever I was making music via a DAW. Sonically, those records were essentially collages assembled on my laptop using manipulated samples and a few midi synths to glue everything together. My main goal was to provide a soundscape for texts that I wrote while doing research as a visual artist. While working on those projects, my appetite for music-making grew exponentially and I pretty soon realized that I didn’t really enjoy being stuck in front of a screen. Basically, I missed the interaction with a “real” instrument. So, halfway through the making of Ripari Minimi I decided to go back to the guitar, my primary instrument, which I had literally not touched for ten years. I understood that focusing on an instrument could have been good for me. It was a time in my life in which I needed to engage in activities that required more practice and manual dexterity. Also, I was after a change in my approach to art too, looking for something that could fit in and resonate more with my daily life. For all these reasons the guitar, its rediscovery and study, felt like the perfect choice. This is pretty much the path that led me to Otto Studi and to its reductionist approach which feels both like an achievement and a liberation. The eight pieces are named after locations—Tourrières, Chalap, Vialas, Sénéchas, and others—rather than concepts, stories, or characters. Were these titles intended as simple markers of time and place, or do they suggest a form of sonic cartography in which each study becomes linked to a particular landscape and moment of listening? They are just markers, nothing more. The family of my partner owns a house in the Cévennes, a fairly wild area in the south of the Massif Central in France, where I spend time every summer. I’ve always been fascinated and inspired by the landscape of the area, especially of the Mount Lozère, a massive plateau with rocky conformations that hold a strong sculptural quality. Otto Studi has been entirely recorded and assembled in the area and it is definitely influenced by it. The titles of the tracks are places where I hanged around or hiked while recording the album. I simply associated the names of the locations to the tracks according to personal moods and feelings. On social media you described Otto Studi as “the discovery of a new path awaiting exploration.” What exactly felt new to you during the making of these recordings? Was it a different relationship with the guitar itself, with improvisation, or with silence and restraint as compositional tools? Well, first of all I recorded the whole thing in a few days, which is already something entirely new for me considering that I’ve always been quite slow with all my previous projects. I must say that before Otto Studi I had already recorded and dismissed a couple of guitar based albums so I guess it was just a matter of time but still, such spontaneity felt very refreshing. Also, through Otto Studi I found a modus operandi, a combination of improvisation and composition, that suits me and that I can now apply to different contexts and approaches to the instrument. Finally, I’ve been working for quite some time on a guitar sound – a balance of melody and noise, shape and deconstruction, accident and control – that I simply couldn’t achieve. With Otto Studi something unlocked, allowing me to reach a territory of creative comfort where I can dwell. Imbriani A recurring theme across your artistic work—whether through Discipula’s visual research, the speculative narratives of The Weaver, or the domestic spaces explored in Imbriani and Ripari Minimi—has been an attention to what lies beneath the visible surface. In Materia Breve, Luca Lanfredi’s accompanying poem speaks of meaning emerging from “the long-lasting breach between things” and of reality being infinitely porous. Do you see Otto Studi as another way of exploring those interstices, this time without words, through small sonic gestures and the spaces between sounds? I find it very nice that you mentioned Lanfredi’s poem from Materia Breve. Vittorio Guindani is, in fact, not only a good friend but also a collaborator and an inspiration for me. This said, I think you really got the point. As I mentioned in my reply to your first question, a few years ago I reached a point in which I felt the need to move away from the speculative narratives I’ve been dealing with before (both in music and visual arts) and somehow focus on the observation of life, pure and simple. Ripari Minimi and Imbriani are both steps in this direction, although strongly self centered. Through the sonic language of Otto Studi I’m starting to reflect on something more universal: the here and now as well as the tiny nuances and epiphanies of everyday life which is the ultimate source of mystery and magic. (Gianmarco Del Re)

These sonic windows shift with every listen, drifting and cascading with restless energy, layered vocal manipulations, and deeply infectious grooves. Vocal fragments that quietly bind every groove with fluid cohesion Such a fitting title for Billion One‘s latest on Woodland Creatures‘ Biome series—every release connected to one of Earth’s distinct bioregions and ecosystems. These sonic windows shift with every listen, drifting and cascading with restless energy, layered vocal manipulations, and deeply infectious grooves. Broken downtempo rhythms weave through pockets of sound design that feel rugged, earthy, and constantly in motion. Multi-instrumentalist Sven Strohschnieder‘s alias thrives within this abundant landscape, and the liner notes aptly describe these excursions as “Balearic downtempo to 80s coded pastoral electronica forays and off to heavy thuds of quasi slowed electro.” We couldn’t agree more. The fertile grounds explored by Billion One feel fully charged, primed for lift-off. A wonderfully unhurried collection, Hi Cozy Paradise opens with flowing, beat-heavy echoes on “Shimmering Heights,” its irresistible groove taking shape from first moments as it eases listeners into this fourteen-track foray. Kaleidoscopic sonic layers continually expand and envelop, yet standout moments often arrive in concise bursts, none more satisfying than micro-funk gem “Sounds Like You,” where stacked vocal lines and synth flourishes recall those wonderfully warped vocal treatments Tobias Lilja has long mastered. Elsewhere, microscopic details and time-stretched voices inhabit technoid flutter on “The Practise Of Not Thinking,” while Clark-inspired brittleness defines “Void,” launching skyward with melodic precision and crystalline momentum. Closing pieces “Glue” and “Forms & Figures” circle back toward vintage Mouse on Mars-style acrobatics, full of playful glitch work and beautifully fractured distortion, all held together by finely threaded vocal fragments that quietly bind every groove with fluid cohesion. Hi Cozy Paradise is available on Woodland Creatures. [Bandcamp] Hi Cozy Paradise by Billion One

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Well, this debut release came literally out of the wild blue yonder, an unexpected gift from my homeland, a sprawling 88-minute tour de force that just may go down as the 2026 Prog surprise of the year. What makes this particularly unique, the band is from my hometown of Miskolc, so this has a personal connection that I cannot and will not dismiss. As per norm in Magyar prog, the talented crew is led by keyboardist/guitarist Jozsef Simko, a tight rhythm section featuring bassist Tibor Kozak and Gergely Sumalan holding down the percussive elements rather perfectly. Add two more special members, a petulant and active Peter Toth on electric guitars and a French expatriate who decided to live in Hungary, Madeline Besson, who sings in perfect English, having been in a band called Molly Moonshine . The production and sound are pristine , the cover wholly attractive and the entire set of songs perched on a delicate balance between technical savvy by the players, and an overt feeling of humility that goes a long way to seduce the prog listener. I felt an immediate sense of maturity within the grooves, a comfort zone that embalmed my space all the way through the 'hidden door' that leads into my soul.The nearly 10-minute opener "Stray Heart" certainly prepares the journey behind the hidden door with an ultra shimmering flurry of electronic serenity, building up into a more petulant variation that had ulterior motives in mind, as both rock riffs and classical movements meld into a platform for introducing Madeline's silky warble, setting the tempo. The harder section seamlessly blend in without to many ruffles , shoveled ahead by basalt bass and demonic drumbeats, the guilty guitars unafraid to use just the right amount of effects, flowing into ambient pools of synthy bliss, before letting the singer emote in a hushed vein. Its pretty and magically soothing."Release" features some of finest violin work heard in ages (Nora Kacsenyak), with mournful cello (Vivien Netti Novak) aching along for the ride, the strings swirling infinitely as if caught in a gentle gale, the piano splendiferous, and a relief of tension that is palpable. It's an accessible prog piece that suggests a liberation that cannot be avoided. An obvious reference to a dearly departed relative (Jozsef's father), becoming quite the eulogy in this case. The gorgeous piano work emphasizes a moment of loving reflection that is worthy of both attention and praise.The mood becomes a tad grimmer on the brooding "Rachel Revisited", a song about domestic abuse from the female viewpoint, an ominous commentary on the weakness of spirit that has poisoned the human condition since the dawn of time. Madeline does a masterful job on the microphone, her crystalline voice appropriately fragile, at times even trembling like a swollen lip. The instrumental presentation is dark and low-key, with progressive accoutrements, scratchy effects and doomsday symphonics that veer towards pain, the splintered guitars quietly shrieking in the front row. Impressive powerful.For a country famous for its thermal waters, as it sits in a massive underground aquafer, and yet has no access whatsoever to any ocean or sea, "Coastline" can only refer to Lake Balaton or the Danube River. The spotlight is a delightfully intimate saxophone solo (Peter Czako) that should put wind to many a sail, a common site on the Hungarian Sea as the Balaton is often referred to. Yet the theme chooses to describe the vagaries of human relationships, the perpetual roller coaster ride of control and miscommunication, suddenly challenged by loving laughter and tender moments.Then, the stylistics take a huge turn into even more progressive exercises , we land on a trio of megalithic epics. Clocking in a colossal 27 minutes and change, "The Brother of Sleep" stamps the prog seal of classification without any hint of hesitation. The inspiration emanates from Oscar Wilde's "The Happy Prince", a rollicking storyline that injects slick percussion, tinges of harpsichord and an airy opening introduction, before eventually turning the rhythm section into on propulsion mode, the vocal gymnastics breathtaking as they lead and harmony voices intertwine. Another gear is put into motion as the echoing chorus becomes escorted by a sweeping organ motif drawing 'silver ribbons'. The third section has a harder drum pattern to rely on, a metallic shroud in the arrangement that underlines a restrained instrumental prowess that paints quite the canvas. The brazen bass is lovingly up-front and center in determining the shifting sonic transmission, settling into an explosive symphonic climax. Very cool opus."The Other Side" wishes to convey a sense of universality, reminding us of the benefits of respecting cultural identities, not surprising in lieu of the unicity of the Magyar ethnicity. The handclaps underline a communal environment as if sitting around a campfire, singing songs, sharing stories and playing music. Can there be a finer panacea, and a better embodiment of peace ? I think not and know of none better!This four-part suite evokes the Book of Revelation, the quarter of an hour epic "Riders" closes the curtain on the now open door, with a wondrous sonic adventure, where light and darkness somehow dare to co-exist. There is little doubt that here the progressive elements really gallop along nicely, like the valiant horses on the Puszta plain, imagining whips cracking the air, and Puli dogs doing their magical herding. Jozsef's elegant piano exudes a prototypical Magyar melancholia, a heady cocktail often mixed with a hint of stubbornness, playful pride and profound emotional commitment. The Peter Toth guitar solo is an ideal example, genuinely sorrowful at first and then building up into a taciturn frenzy without going deliberately crazy. The ambient piano mid-section is drop-dead beautiful, the solitude broken by a lone bass elevation that alters the pace into a bluesy organ-led adventure where Madeline gets to sing her thoughts. The upward staircase of sound rises inexorably to its mighty conclusion, with a grandiose final section, majestic and imperious , reaching for the heavens , a magnificent pinnacle that seals the deal.One of the finer debut heard in many a moon, what really stands out is the utter humbleness expressed throughout ,and in our increasingly turbulent noise factory society, this has been quite a soothing experience that should bear many future releases in the future. Highly recommended with or without a glass of palinka.4.5 fractured coils

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — 2025 brought the exciting news that Swedish female-fronted prog band Paatos had not only regrouped, but were ready to deliver a brand new studio work. `Timeloss', their debut from 2002, was a minor modern prog classic, effortlessly blending gloomy rock, weary jazz, hypnotic ambience and even glitching trip-hop and electronica. The departure of early guitarist Reine Fiske (finding success with alt-rockers Dungen) only slightly affected their sound, with the group retaining the sullen atmospheres but adopting more of an alternative rock/intelligent pop approach, even attracting to attention of modern prog notable Steven Wilson enough to work on their second album `Kallocain'.Thirteen years on from their last work, the same line-up since 2011's `Breathing' now offers `Ligament', and it shows the band continuing to experiment and break new ground, whilst also retaining all the subtle dynamics, melancholic moods, bursts of power and air of mystery that permeated all their previous works. Murky cinematic rock, wilting ballads, eerie distortions and freeform jams all blur together, and it even boasts a guest appearance from Mikael Akerfeldt of progressive-minded metal act Opeth.Launching to a cavalcade of Huxflux Nettermalm's breakneck drumming, opener `Chemical Escape' hits the ground running, all frantic energy and rattling bluster with a muscular chorus. Ulf Ivarsson's gorgeously murmuring, grooving bass (front and center the entire album) and Peter Nylander's shimmering guitars with grinding King Crimson-like reaching strains get mangled together, and while Petronella Nettermalm sighs and breathily coos "I'll be perfectly alright", the slinking and skittering electronic/drum-n-bass breakdown and stark violin scratches in the climax suggest overwise.The relentless `Beyond the Forest' is too up-tempo to be a traditional ballad, rather it's a darkly sultry duet between Petronella and Opeth's Mikael Akerfeldt that's full of longing...and a definite hint of danger. Wrapping around their voices is creaking cello and grand Mellotron rises, and the dark ambient outro ends on a very ambiguous note - is the piece about two lovers passionately pining for each-other, or is one of them trying to escape the dangerously obsessed other? You be the judge.Reflective and evocative ballad `I Deny' tiptoes with crystalline piano and ringing guitars that glisten with pristine beauty. Short but not even slightly sweet, the two-minute title-track is a breakneck runaway tantrum of noise, Petronella's voice a distorted snarl writhing around barb-wire guitars, and `Post War Liminal' is a lurching, stop-start staccato drone that wouldn't have sounded out of place on a Bass Communion album.Opening to weeping Mellotron veils, `I'm Letting Go' is a powerful yet reflective indie pop-rocker that soars with hope thanks to Petronella's defiant and rousing vocal. While her spectral voice looms and soars around `Who Am I', it's hard to relax with how `off' in parts the piece sounds, crumbling into the embers of a jazz-fusion improvisation, all scratching and scraping distortion, abrasive effects, ghostly and discordant piano and grumbling guitar trembles before its equally uneasy ambient close.`November' is a reflective lament around the gentlest of jazz patterings and lowly cavernous reverberations. But siren calls and angelic harmonies are quickly ripped to shreds with the violent `Last Ones of Our Kind', a raging political attack that ripples with danger and breathless tension. Patronella warns there's "no redemption to the found", and while offering one of the more overtly obvious and striking chorus moments of the disc, the band whips up a suitably stormy noise with multiple improvised passages of wavering keyboard swirls, crushing drums and blistering guitar salvos, sounding not unlike moments of Steven Wilson's solo works.Lurking closer `Svart' presses down heavy on the listener and refuses to remove its boot, a mucky gothic dirge that, despite the most minuscule glimpses of hope and respite, grumbles with a Magma/Zuehl-like oppression with its pounding percussion and dingy gulping bass. What, you thought with lyrics like the "Nothing will remain, nothing with live..." that the band would end on smiles and sunshine?!With this latest work, the band achieves a near-perfect balance of new directions and expected intense atmospheres that are still instantly recognisable as Paatos, but they are now not afraid to unsettle or move away from the more melodic, tune-based material of several of their last few releases. Petronella's voice has never been so powerful, and the instrumental interplay from the fellas has never moved so seamlessly from complex to subtle. It means `Ligament' is their darkest, most daring and experimental release yet, and certainly their strongest and most exciting effort since their debut.Welcome back, Paatos - four stars.(please note - `Port War Liminal' and `November' seem to be sadly absent from the LP release)

items.body: For more than three decades, Ataraxia has been regarded as both a household name and a cult act within the broad realms of Ethereal, Neo-Classical, Folk, and related musical genres. Throughout the years, Ataraxia’s core members – Francesca Nicoli, Vittorio Vandelli, and Giovanni Pagliari – have remained driven by an inexhaustible source of inspiration, deeply rooted in their spiritual experience. Of course, their remarkable talent plays a vital role, but so does the authenticity that consistently shines through in their compositions. Ataraxia offers a genuine remedy – perhaps even an antidote – to a world that rushes by like a bullet train. Ataraxia embodies reflection and wisdom, a profound love of nature, and a deep respect for ancient traditions, legends, and myths. With their latest album, “Sylfaera The Fair”, released through the Greek label The Circle Music and serving as the concluding chapter of a new trilogy, Ataraxia once again affirm not only their artistic brilliance but also the sincerity and integrity that define their approach to music. For me, Ataraxia’s “Sylfaera The Fair” is a truly immersive experience – one in which spirituality and artistry become inseparable. I had the pleasure of discussing the album and much more with Francesca Nicoli. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Ataraxia interview Q: Ataraxia was formed almost 40 years ago, and your latest album marks the thirtieth full-length release in this impressive journey. How do you look back on the young artists you were in the 1980s, and what has remained the common thread throughout this long career? Francesca: The first Ataraxia album was born in 1990, 36 years ago. We cannot describe a thirty-six-year process because we are always looking toward the so-called future; we are always looking ahead to what we will do. It has been such a fast, intense, and prolific flow that we are unable to find descriptive phrases that allow us to reflect on the complete body of work, because this is nothing other than the complete work of our life brought into music. We remember the experiences and enthusiasm of concerts around the world, the recording of the albums, but our emotions and vision are all directed toward what will be. Perhaps one day, a listener will be able to outline the path; we are the same people who have lived thirty different lives, so by necessity, we are others while maintaining that original root. It is as if we had been reincarnated 30 times in different bodies while maintaining the same soul that discovers new possibilities every time. Q: “Sylfaera The Fair” is the final part of an Ataraxia trilogy preceded by “Pomegranate” (2022) and “Centaurea” (2024). Did you know from the very beginning that it was going to be a trilogy, or did this happen more along the way? And what does this final opus represent, and how should listeners approach the trilogy as a whole? Francesca: We didn’t know it for sure, but we felt it; we knew it would end this way because we have always worked in trilogies throughout our career. It represents a part of our life in a mythological key, and therefore accessible to all and useful to everyone, like any form of art, to sublimate the meaning of existence for those who listen to it. The right approach is simply to listen to it in order, or even in reverse—from the third album to the first—and let the images that accompany the listening bloom, take the journey, enjoy the journey, and see how one comes out transformed by all this. A musical listening is always a journey, and from no journey nobody returns the same and to the same place. Q: Trilogies originated in antiquity, and I remain fascinated by how this format continues to evolve today. What fascinates you personally about the trilogy form, the symbols (like the number 9 in this album) in it and are there any examples from the wider art world that have particularly inspired or moved you? Francesca: The number three is a peculiar number, the number of perfection and communication. Cycles are completed that start from one, which also corresponds to the sign of Aries, and therefore to birth, the initial force that brings life to bloom and utter its first cry. Then, two is the mirror; we are in front of another who reflects our essence—without which we would not know who we are—up to the completeness of three, which is communication and creation, because from the union of two is born; the son, or what is created; by the energy of the two, becoming something new. Needless to say, Tolkien has always inspired us, and Tolkien also worked with the trilogy. But there are also references in painting and an interesting numerological studies we did years ago. Nine is the maximum expression of three (3×3), and nine are the characters of the album who will find themselves energetically creating “Sylfaera The Fair”, the realm of music, beauty, and harmony. Nine is the Hermit of the Tarot, the one who in solitude carries the lamp of knowledge on a path backwards, walking toward the past, in retrocausality. Then we have the Tesla sequence 3-6-9, which is a complement of mathematical and philosophical awareness that has always fascinated us. Q: I believe it is fair to say that mysticism has always played a central role in Ataraxia‘s musical universe and that it also reflects something about the people behind the artists. How important is the mystical dimension in your daily lives, and how do you perceive mysticism in the contemporary Western world, where it seems to be gradually disappearing? Francesca: We were born with this mystical nature, and since we were children, we have lived experiences linked to subtle worlds, amplified by life in medieval villages or on the Apennines of our region. Woods, rivers, mountains, and undoubtedly our numerous experiences on the Greek islands, as well as those on the Italian peaks, have created the substrate—the most powerful means—to experience our music in a mystical state. The mystical dimension in everyday life is still our nature; it is not a specific moment we dedicate ourselves to, it is the very way in which we perceive life and our experiences. We struggle to give you explanations regarding the disappearance of mysticism in the contemporary Western world because we live things from the inside; we exist in this dimension 24 hours a day, and this is our lens. In a certain way, staying within this dimension protects us—otherwise, we would not be able to write music, to feel in a certain way, or to imagine a profound bond between everything and between this and other possible dimensions. For us, mysticism is nothing more than feeling a profound connection, at both a cellular level and a higher mental level, to the heart of things, to the heart of a greater design that gives meaning to this earthly experience. A profound sensitivity is necessary, which can be wounded by the prosaic nature of life, and we must take care of it every day. Q: Ataraxia’s music often evokes ancient civilizations, forgotten rituals, and a sacred experience of nature, an atmosphere strengthened by the use of traditional instruments. How essential is this approach to your artistic identity, and how do you view modern music culture and the rise of AI, which in some ways seems to represent its opposite? Francesca: The nature of our music is as you describe; this approach is essential to be able to express ourselves in an honest, authentic way, which can bring forth sincere suggestions. Our creativity is indomitable, so we do not need ‘external intelligences’; due to a lack of inspiration; furthermore, we have been in the musical world for so many years that we feel no need for it at all. We like working with new sounds (natural and synthesized), but not delegating. We like having the responsibility for what we do, being the conductors of the orchestra, and using and refining our musical intelligence in order to remain operative and lucid. We don’t set ourselves against something; we act creatively to create something. Q: Speaking of traditional instruments, “Sylfaera The Fair” is once again an absolute masterpiece and a true tour de force, featuring contributions from guest musicians. How do you bring such an ambitious undertaking to life, and what does the composition process look like in practice? Francesca: For us, it is completely natural because every time, fellow musician friends arrive who integrate into the new project and the new album in a completely spontaneous way, and everything flows. We don’t have to tell them what to do or what not to do; they intuit it perfectly and create their melodies, blending their musical experience with our suggestions. Then, we work with great concentration on the rhythmic parts because we create them ourselves; these create the earth upon which the air and the water of the instruments move, and the fire—the Flame—is the union of all these forces in harmony, working toward a single goal: the creation of the specific dimension of this musical micro-universe that’s the album. Q: Were there any specific innovations or evolutions in the choice of instruments or in the overall production process during the creation of this trilogy and especially the latest album? Francesca: The first album of the trilogy, “Pomegranate”, utilized the simplicity of our essential instruments: classical and electric guitar, keyboards, cello, and voice, with few rhythmic patterns. It was an essential and poetic album. The second album of the trilogy, “Centaurea”, became enriched with more complex arrangements while maintaining the same instruments, to which drum patterns of a certain importance were added, varying the musical suggestions as we explored different genres (Folk ballads, Neo-Classical arias, more symphonic tracks, Dream-Pop, etc.). The new album focuses on a first part more closely linked to Nordic and Mediterranean Folk, introducing uilleann pipes, bodhrán, flutes, massive tribal percussion, and choirs, while the second part is more in line with our previous releases. Q: After releasing 30 Ataraxia albums, I wonder whether there are still artists or records that continue to inspire you. More broadly, what do inspiration and creativity mean when you have devoted so many years to the same artistic project? How have these concepts evolved for you over time, and how do you continue to nurture them? Francesca: Certainly, there are artists who inspire us greatly; they don’t directly inspire our music, but rather our soul. We are always listening to new music that we discover along the way, and music remains the soundtrack of our emotions. Since we were children, we have experienced creativity as a form of expression, as the natural nourishment of our own existences, and so now we are that expression—it is our DNA. Music is our language, our universe, our way of communicating with ourselves and with what surrounds us. Everything has evolved along with our life experiences, our maturity, our spiritual search, our sufferings, and our discoveries. We nourish it simply by living and experiencing the universe of life. Q: Glossolalia, or the use of imaginary language, has long played a role in your work and seems to fit naturally within the spiritual dimension of Ataraxia. How do you approach this practice creatively? Does it require a particular form of introspection, meditation, or discipline, and have you noticed an evolution in this aspect of your work over the years? Francesca: I have always used different ancient and modern languages in my lyrics, and there has always been a track in glossolalia on every album. Each language I used was chosen for the peculiarity of its sound, which suited that specific piece of music, and from there, the step to glossolalia is a short one. Usually, I listen to the compositions the band proposes and instinctively work on the vocal melodies, which already have a specific color connected to particular sounds. It is like a meditative process: I close my eyes, listen, and the sounds come out one after the other without any particular construction—they emerge spontaneously. It seems like a magical process; in reality, the voice becomes like a musical instrument that produces sounds articulated into words. The technique has been the same since the beginning, only in this latest album it was used much more extensively compared to the previous ones. Q: What are the current short-term plans for Ataraxia, and what can we expect from the band in the longer term? Francesca: In the short term, we are working on the live performance of this album experience—each time different, each time linked to the venue and the situation in which we will be performing. In the long term, we do not know yet. Everything is revealed to us along the path, just like breathing: we inhale, just as when releasing an album, we inhale to recharge with oxygen, which will allow us to exhale a new opus once again. About Ataraxia Ataraxia is a neoclassical dark wave and dark folk band from Modena and Reggio Emilia in northern Italy. The group was founded in the second half of the 1980s by vocalist Francesca Nicoli and guitarist Michele Urbano, with the line-up stabilising around Nicoli, guitarist and composer Vittorio Vandelli, and keyboardist Giovanni Pagliari in the early 1990s. Their work combines electronic technology with archaic and acoustic instruments, and their lyrics frequently reference nature, ancient cultures and mythological themes, often performed in historically resonant locations. In their first years Ataraxia issued self-released recordings such as “Prophetia” and “Nosce Te Ipsum” before working with labels including Energeia and Cruel Moon International, gradually building an extensive discography across cassette, CD and vinyl formats. Late-1990s albums such as “Historiae” explored medieval and liturgical atmospheres; the album was later issued by Ark Records and documented both studio and live recordings, including material captured in a medieval court in 1998. During the 2000s the band continued to refine its blend of neoclassical, ethereal and folk-influenced material on releases like “Suenos” and “Os Cavaleiros do Templo,” with several titles later revisited. Twilight Records reissued long-deleted works including “Saphir” and “Os Cavaleiros do Templo.” In 2016 Ataraxia released “Deep Blue Firmament” via Sleaszy Rider Records. Subsequent full-lengths included “Synchronicity Embraced” (2018) and “Quasar” (stylised as “ΘUASAR”). The collaboration with The Circle Music began with the 28th studio album “Pomegranate (The Chant of the Elementals)”, released in 2022 on digital, CD and vinyl formats. Ahead of that album the band issued several videos, including “Hlara Aralh” and “Aura Magi.” Pomegranate – The Chant Of The Elementals by Ataraxia Ataraxia’s 29th studio album “Centaurea” followed in 2024, again on The Circle Music in digital, CD and vinyl editions. Singles and videos from this period included “The Source,” “Galen,” “Viriditas,” “Coelestis” and “Ignis Pater.” Centaurea by Ataraxia And now there is the band’s 30th album “Sylfaera the Fair”.

items.body: Aesthetische, the Brazilian electronic duo, released the digital EP “Every Beat Matters” on June 26, 2026 through Alfa Matrix. The “Every Beat Matters” EP collects four tracks and three remixes of “Chew The Loop”, and carries an explicit anti-extremism message. Aesthetische bring a sound that mixes EBM, industrialized future pop and dancefloor electronics, with machine rhythms, synth hooks and forceful vocals. Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi cite Front Line Assembly and Front 242 as touchstones. Every Beat Matters EP by AESTHETISCHE Aesthetische’s ‘Every Beat Matters’: tracks and message “Every Beat Matters” runs four tracks – “Break The State”, “Thirty Two Percent”, “Chew The Loop” and “Parallel Worlds” – followed by three remixes of “Chew The Loop”: the “beat the loop remix”, a “shortmix version” and the “spit the loop mix”. Alfa Matrix previewed “Chew The Loop” on its compilation “Sounds From The Matrix 026”, released on June 19, 2026. The EP ties its title to a stance against authoritarian rhetoric, fascism, war and prejudice, framing “every beat matters” as a call for awareness, resistance and unity; the campaign artwork carries the lines “Extremism has no place here” and “FCK NZS”. The label describes the record as turning “a simple message into a powerful call for awareness, resistance and unity.” The theme follows earlier Aesthetische records: the 2022 album “rvprty” was issued as a stand against far-right, anti-science and anti-democratic movements. About Aesthetische Aesthetische is the project of Brazilian musicians Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi, both previously in the electro-industrial act Aghast View. The duo formed this project in 2012 and have released through the Belgian label Alfa Matrix since their debut. Their albums include “Powerswitch” (2012), “HybridCore” (2014), “Co3xist3ns3” (2019) and “rvprty” (2022), alongside a run of EPs and singles. In recent years the duo released the EP “Confidence Is Silent” in 2024 and the EP “Selling Fear” in 2025, the latter also drawing on the legacy of Front Line Assembly and Front 242. Aesthetische have also discussed their approach with Side-Line in a 2024 interview. “Every Beat Matters”, released on June 26, 2026, extends the duo’s record of pairing club-focused EBM with anti-authoritarian themes.

items.body: Alfa Matrix has released Unter Null’s “The Rise From Ruin (and the Ritual of Becoming)” on June 26, 2026 as a limited double-CD digipak with an extended booklet, and as a download via Bandcamp. The set revisits the early Erica Dunham period of the project and is available now as a digital pre-order on Bandcamp and as a physical pre-order through the Alfa Matrix Store. At the centre of the release is “The Failure Epiphany”, the Alfa Matrix album that helped launch Unter Null’s early dark electro and industrial profile. The second disc expands that period with material from the EPs “Sick Fuck”, “Sacrament”, and “Absolution”, plus remixes by Noisuf-X vs. X-Fusion, Manufactura, T3chnophobia, Aslan Faction, Grendel, KiEw, Terrorfakt, and C-Drone-Defect. The release holds 34 tracks in total. The Rise From Ruin (and the Ritual of Becoming) (Deluxe Edition) by UNTER NULL About Unter Null Unter Null is the solo project of American musician Erica Dunham, founded in 1998 in Seattle, Washington. Initially rooted in power noise and harsh electronics, the project evolved into aggrotech/dark elektro through early self-released material and live dates in the early 2000s. Unter Null’s first full-length album, “The Failure Epiphany”, arrived in 2005 via Alfa Matrix (later re-issued with bonus material), following club traction around “Your Nightmare” and “Sick Fuck”. Touring in the U.S. and Europe followed in 2005–2006. On December 25, 2008, a house/studio fire destroyed Dunham’s recording equipment and jeopardized work then in progress. Despite the loss, files were recovered and Unter Null released “Moving On” in 2010 (Alfa Matrix), including expanded editions and international versions. Dunham later relocated for a period to Hamburg, Germany, before activity shifted again to the U.S. Pacific Northwest. The project continued sporadic releases and remixes through the 2010s. She also worked on her more atmospheric side project Stray in that period. In 2025, Unter Null returned with new studio material through Alfa Matrix, including the single “Coming Up To Breathe” (April 4, 2025) and the EP “You Made A Monster” (July 25, 2025). The EP features remixes by C-Lekktor, Leaether Strip, and Frontal Boundary and is distributed digitally via Bandcamp and other platforms. Unter Null also contributed remixes and collaborations in 2025, including featured work connected to Frontal Boundary.

items.body: LAHO, the Finnish dark electronic project of Konsta Vehkala, released the seven-track album “Death Machines” on June 26, 2026. The digital release gathers three of the project’s 2026 singles with four new tracks, among them a cover of Depeche Mode’s “Behind the Wheel”. LAHO blends industrial, EBM, futurepop and darkwave, with lyrics centred on dystopian themes and the darker side of human behaviour. Vehkala writes, programs and produces the project alone from Jyväskylä, Finland. “Death Machines” is the first LAHO album to feature vocals. Vehkala built the project’s earlier catalogue as instrumental work before resuming LAHO in 2024 after a 13-year break. The single “Programmed”, released on February 12, 2026, opened the new phase, followed by the singles “The Great Collapse” and “Last Rays of the Sun”. Death Machines by LAHO LAHO ‘Death Machines’ tracklist and the Depeche Mode cover “Death Machines” runs seven tracks: “Programmed”, “The Great Collapse”, “Cold New World”, “Decimated Memories”, “Fading Out”, “Last Rays of the Sun” and “Behind the Wheel”. The first, second and sixth tracks appeared earlier as standalone singles, while the other four are new to the album. The closing track reworks Depeche Mode’s “Behind the Wheel”, written by Martin L. Gore and first issued on the 1987 album “Music for the Masses”. Vehkala recorded, programmed and produced the album himself. He has tied the project’s lyrics to technology and modern life, describing the opening single “Programmed” as “a heavy hitting electronic track about our life in the ever-growing synthetic world.” The album is available digitally through Bandcamp. About LAHO LAHO is the solo project of Finnish musician and recording engineer Konsta Vehkala, based in Jyväskylä. It began in 2006 under the name Lahonnut Konkelo, a run of electronic and industrial experiments, with the name soon shortened to LAHO. The first EP, “The Other Side”, appeared in 2007 as a self-released CDr and was later reissued by the Italian netlabel Ekleipsi. Ekleipsi also issued the debut album “Escape from the Dying Star” in April 2009, a ten-track record made between 2007 and 2008 that mixed electro-industrial, synth work and distorted guitar. Vehkala followed it with the standalone track “The World in Flames” (2009), the single “Mechanigod” (2011) and the one-off digital release “Walking in the Air (1984 mix)” in December 2021. The project then went quiet for 13 years while Vehkala focused on other work. He resumed writing for LAHO in 2024 and added vocals as a permanent element, ending a previously instrumental catalogue. The 2026 singles “Programmed”, “The Great Collapse” and “Last Rays of the Sun” introduced the new direction. Alongside LAHO, Vehkala plays drums in the Finnish melodic metal band Psychework and has performed and recorded with Gian, Vipermilk and Lojohh, while contributing recording, mixing and mastering work to other Finnish acts. “Death Machines”, released on June 26, 2026, is the project’s first vocal-led album and its first full-length since 2009.

items.body: Teanga Teanga released the single “Around the World” worldwide on June 26, 2026. The project pairs New York art-pop artist Pamela Sue Mann with Dublin composer-producer Paul Murphy, who records as pxmurphy. Their version reworks “Around the World,” the 1956 standard, through synthesizers, electronics and strings rather than orchestral pop. Teanga Teanga rework a 1956 standard The single reinterprets “Around the World,” the title song from the 1956 film “Around the World in 80 Days.” Victor Young wrote the music and Harold Adamson the lyrics; Nat King Cole recorded a vocal version, one of several covers of the song. Teanga Teanga rebuild the track with cinematic synths, spectral textures, spoken passages and sweeping strings, with Mann on lead vocals. Murphy said the recording grew out of studio sessions and file-sharing between the two. “We suddenly got inspired by something,” he stated. “If we both buzz off it, we start digging in and seeing what comes out.” Mann described her approach to covering a standard: “If you’re going to do a cover, you’ve got to have something soulful — depth, honesty, empathy. Otherwise you’re just doing a cover.” The pair call the recording “time travel through music.” “Around the World” is available on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. The duo released an official video for “Around the World”, which streams on YouTube: About Teanga Teanga Teanga Teanga is the collaborative project of Pamela Sue Mann and Paul Murphy. Mann is a singer-songwriter, pianist, producer and poet based in New York and a graduate of Berklee College of Music. She released her self-titled album in 1999 and has recorded and toured with Suzanne Vega, Donna Lewis, Gerry Leonard and producer David Baron. Murphy, based in Dublin, co-founded Electric Penguins, whose debut album “Goodbye from the Electric Penguins” appeared in 2006. NPR featured the band, and BBC Radio London presenter Robert Elms named the single “Highgate Hill” his track of the year. Murphy also composes for television and advertising, and Electric Penguins released the album “The Way Lights a Fire” in June 2025. Mann and Murphy recorded “Around the World” remotely, the single now carrying their work forward under the Teanga Teanga name.

items.body: dreDDup, the industrial project from Novi Sad, Serbia, released a music video for the song “President Evil” on June 28, 2026. The dreDDup “President Evil” clip is the third single taken from the album “Pan/Dora” and, according to the band, the fourth dreDDup video made with AI technology, directed by founder Mihajlo Obrenov. The band brings a sound that mixes EBM, industrial and electronics, with distorted vocals and heavy programming; the band describes “President Evil” as an EBM/industrial track. Obrenov writes and produces the project from Novi Sad. Pan/Dora by dreDDup dreDDup’s ‘President Evil’ and the ‘Pan/Dora’ album “President Evil” is the tenth track on “Pan/Dora”, the band’s eleventh studio album, issued in 2024 and recorded at DURU Studio in Novi Sad. The band has framed the record as the start of a planned trilogy. Mihajlo Obrenov directed the video and built it with AI tools, continuing a run that began with the 2023 single “Clark Can’t“, the project’s first AI video, followed by “Cherry Noble” and “Not From Here“. The band states it plans two more videos for songs from “Pan/Dora” and is recording its next album. dreDDup also says it will mark 30 years of activity in 2027. About dreDDup dreDDup formed in 1997 in Novi Sad, Serbia, founded by Mihajlo Obrenov, who also records as miKKa, with drummer Robert Sabadoš. The project mixes industrial, EBM and electronics, and Obrenov has long described the sound as “demonic electronic”. Alongside the project, Obrenov runs the online label Crime:Scene Records, which he started in 2008, and the experimental project MRT, whose eleventh album “Kerrang” appeared in 2024. The band built a long catalogue across nearly three decades, reaching its eleventh studio album with “Pan/Dora” in 2024. From late 2023 the project paired new singles with AI-assisted videos, among them “Clark Can’t”, “Cherry Noble” and “Not From Here”. “President Evil”, released as a video on June 28, 2026, is the third single drawn from “Pan/Dora” and arrives as the band approaches its 30th year in 2027.

items.body: Miseria Ultima, the Finnish dark electro duo signed to Alfa Matrix, are working on a new album, the follow-up to their excellent 2024 record “Arctic Esotericism“. The Miseria Ultima new album is in progress, with the duo advancing to the mixing stage and returning to the studio at the end of June 2026. Miseria Ultima bring a dark electro sound that mixes aggrotech and EBM, built on harsh beats and distorted vocals. Aleksi Martikainen handles vocals and Kimmo Huhtala the synths. The duo previewed the new material with “Northern Skin”, a track on the Alfa Matrix compilation Sounds From The Matrix 026, released on June 19, 2026, which collects previews of songs from releases due later in the year. Miseria Ultima’s new album and studio work Martikainen says the duo are “slowly advancing to mixing phase” and would “head back to studio at the end of this month” for further work on the songs. And he adds: “The new album we are working on carries themes and anthems of the North, continuing the path we began before with a blend of mellow, striking synths and cold melodies. items.body: Stars and the Underground, the New Zealand project of Auckland musician John Mason, released the single “Echolocation” on May 22, 2026. The Stars and the Underground “Echolocation” single features guest vocals from Hannah Berry of the Auckland dark-electronic project Talmar, and is the second single trailing the band’s forthcoming debut album “Guardians of the Night”. Stars and the Underground bring a sound that mixes post-punk, shoegaze and dark synth wave, with chiming guitars, low basslines and reverb-heavy vocals. John Mason handles vocals, guitars and bass, while John McDermott plays drums and produces. Echolocation by Stars and the Underground Stars and the Underground revisit ‘Echolocation’ with Talmar “Echolocation” is a reworked version of a song the band first issued on the limited “Evolution Circle EP” in 2019. For the 2026 single, the track was re-recorded with Hannah Berry of Talmar added on vocals. John McDermott recorded, mixed and mastered it at Arch Hill Studios in Auckland. The single follows “Lonely Black Hearts”, released on April 1, 2025, and both tracks point to the album “Guardians of the Night”. “While we have faced various challenges, I believe this has ultimately contributed to a stronger final product,” Mason stated. “‘Echolocation’ is a testament to this, as we initially introduced the concept in the limited release of the Evolution Circle EP. We chose to revisit the song, highlighting John McDermott’s exceptional drumming and production skills, along with Hannah’s enchanting contributions that elevate the track to new ethereal heights.” The video for “Echolocation” runs on the band’s official YouTube channel: About Stars and the Underground Stars and the Underground is a New Zealand project built around Auckland musician John Mason, who founded it in 2019. The current line-up pairs Mason on vocals, guitars and bass with John McDermott on drums and production; McDermott records the project at his Arch Hill Studios in Auckland. According to the band, Mason previously played in the New Zealand goth-rock group Winterland and McDermott in the Headless Chickens. The project debuted in 2019 with the “Evolution Circle EP”, which carried the first version of “Echolocation”. After a gap, the band returned on April 1, 2025 with the single “Lonely Black Hearts”, issued with remixes as the first single from the forthcoming debut album “Guardians of the Night”. “Echolocation”, released on May 22, 2026 with Hannah Berry of Talmar, is the second single drawn from that album. Talmar is the solo project of Auckland visual artist Hannah Berry, who makes dark electronic music.

items.body: Based in Barcelona, SDH (Semiotics Department Of Heteronyms) released their third album this year, marking their first release on Artoffact Records. The album offers ten relatively short tracks that blend a variety of influences. One moment, the music leans toward Electro-Wave; the next, it adopts a harder, Body Pop-inspired edge. Elsewhere, the sound shifts into more Pop-oriented territory, occasionally even embracing Dance elements. As a result, there is plenty to explore and discover throughout the record. Adding to its appeal is the distinctive half-whispered vocal style of Andrea Pérez, which gives the songs an intimate and recognizable character. Every track has something interesting to offer, although I personally find myself most drawn to the harder-hitting compositions. Diversity is undoubtedly the album’s greatest strength, making it accessible to a broad-minded audience with varied musical tastes. My only criticism is that some of the songs feel a little too short, leaving me wanting more. Nevertheless, this remains a highly enjoyable release, filled with memorable moments and several standout tracks. (Rating:8). Listen to “You Lost My Keys”: https://semioticsdepartmentofheteronyms.bandcamp.com/track/you-lost-my-keys

items.body: Andrew Chalk had debuted in 1985 with the free-form industrial noise of his project Ferial Confine, documented on Meiosis (Broken Flag, 1985) and The Full Use Of Nothing (Fusetron, 1985) before evolving into the less extreme soundpainting of First, Second And Third Drop (1986). He also contributed to David Jackman's Organum, and joined the British collective Ora in 1991.Chalk emerged solo with the crystalline, shimmering ambient music of (b>East of the Sun (1997), containing Winter Arc (1994) and The Plain (1996), and soon became a specialist of ringing overtones.His pre-Ora works is documented on two anthologies: Crescent (2000) collects the cassettes Crescent (1986) and Harvest (1988), whereas Tahta Tarla (1993), a collaboration with Giancarlo Toniutti, contains Chalk's Warkswood (1988) as well as Toniutti's Tienalauami.Over the Edges (1999) contains three untiled works of 1997 obtained by exciting only two strings of an acoustic guitar with an e-bow (an experiment along the lines of old ideas by Alvin Lucier and Ellen Fullman). Sumac (1999) documents a 71-minute collaboration from 1997 between Jonathan Coleclough and Andrew Chalk. This Growing Clearing (2004) documents a collaboration between Brendan Walls and Andrew Chalk. Fall In The Wake Of A Flawless Landscape (2004) contains one 41-minute track. The 74-minute two-movement droning symphony of Shadows From The Album Skies (2004), possibly his masterpiece, is devoted to extended droning-guitar monoliths whose overtones hark back to the experiments of Phill Niblock and Eliane Radigue.The River That Flows Into The Sands (2005) and The River That Flows Into The Sands II (2006) explore oneiric and ghostly guitar soundscapes.Blue Eyes Of The March (2006) is a 51-minute suite for solo piano.Mirror is a prolific collaboration between Christoph Heemann and Andrew Chalk that has rarely produced major works. The first one, Eye Of The Storm (1999), built out of manipulated natural sounds, ringing percussion, fluttering electronics and Heeman's sustained bowing drones, would have been enough to make the point. The deluge of releases that followed was hardly justified by the narrow concept: Ringstones (1999), Mirror of The Sea (2000), Front Row Centre (2000), Nightwalkers (2000), The View (2000), Visiting Star (2000), I Paint For Love Of Color (2001), Islands (2001), Nights (2001), Die Spiegelmanufaktur (2002) with Jim O'Rourke, Nights (2002), Solaris (2002), that introduced elements of dissonant avantgarde music, A Pilgrim's Solace (2003), Figures In A Landscape (2004), Places Of Light (2004), Under The Sun (2004), Nightwalkers (2005) with Andreas Martin, Still Valley (2005), the denser Viking Burial For A French Car (2005).Goldfall (2006), one of his best, and the inferior Time Of Hayfield (2007) manipulate piano notes by Vikki Jackman. Vega (2006) turned to a more ethereal atmosphere.The Days After (2007) collects Mirror works from the early 2000s.Isolde is the duo of Andrew Chalk and Robin Barnes that released All Things To Fall Like Marching Men (Penny Poppet, 2005), You're Alone In Red Riding Picture (2005) and On Waving And Drowning (Penny Poppet, 2006).The Cable House (Faraway Press, 2009) creates fragile ghosts of melodies out of piano notes. Half of it is taken up by the 20-minute Naybuchi.In Faxfleet Clouds Uplifted Autumn Gave Passage To Kind Nature (Faraway Press, 2009) documents a collaboration with Daisuke Suzuki (an old Ora collaborator).Ghost of Nakhodka (2009 - Siren, 2010) was an excursion into ambient and minimalist chamber music.Violin By Night (Faraway Press, 2011) produced lyrical drones out of piano, guitar, electronics and field recordings.Echos Pastoraux (La Scie Doree, 2011), credited to Elodie, documents a collaboration between Andrew Chalk and Belgian composer Timo Van Luijk. La Lumiere Parfumee (Faraway Press, 2012) was its follow-up.Andrew Chalk launched the project Marsfield with The Towering Sky (Faraway Press, 2010), recorded with Vikki Jackman, Robin Barnes, and Brendan Walls in 2005, and Three Sunsets Over Marsfield (Faraway Press, 2010), that collects recordings from 2002.(Translation by/ Tradotto da Andrea Marengo)Andrew Chalk aveva debuttato nel 1985 con l'industrial noise free-form del suo progetto Ferial Confine documentato su Meiosis (Broken Flag, 1985) e The Full Use Of Nothing (Fusetron, 1985) prima di progredire nel meno estremo soundpainting di First Second And Third Drop (1986). Egli contribuì a fondare gli Organum di David Jackman, aderendo inoltre al collettivo Ora nel 1991.Chalk debuttò come solista con l'ambient cristallina e scintillante di (b>East Of The Sun (1997), diventando presto uno specialista degli ipertoni squillanti. L'album contiene Winter Arc (1994) e The Oplain (1996). Il suoi lavori pre-Ora sono documentati in due antologie: Crescent (2000), contenente le cassette Crescent (1986) e Harvest (1988), e Tahta Tarla (1993), contenente Tienalaumi (1988) e Warkswood (1988).Over The Edges (1999) contiene tre lavori senza titolo del 1997 ottenuti pizzicando soltanto due corde di una chitarra acustica con un e-bow (un esperimento che segue la scia delle prime idee di Alvin Lucier ed Ellen Fullman). Sumac (1999) documenta una collaborazione di settantuno minuti del 1997 tra Jonathan Coleclough e Andrew Chalk. This Growing Clearing (2004) documenta una collaborazione tra Brendan Walls e Andrew Chalk. Fall In The Wake Of A Flawless Landscape (2004) contiene una traccia di quarantuno minuti. La sinfonia di settantaquattro minuti in due movimenti di Shadows From The Album Skies (2004), probabilmente il suo capolavoro, è fedele ai monoliti estesi della droning guitar mentre gli ipertoni rievocano gli esperimenti di Phill Niblock e Eliane Radigue.The River That Flows Into The Sands (2005) e The river That Flows Into The Sands II (2006) esplorano onirici e spettrali paesaggi sonori per chitarra.Blue Eyes Of The March (2006) è una suite di cinquantuno minuti per solo pianoforte.Mirror è una prolifica collaborazione tra Christoph Heeman ed Andrew Chalk che raramente ha prodotto lavori significativi. Il primo, Eye Of The Storm (1999), costruito adoperando suoni naturali manipolati, percussioni squillanti, elettroniche fluttuanti e i droni inarcati e prolungati di Heeman, conteneva spunti sufficienti per mettere a punto un'idea. L'inondazione di pubblicazioni avrebbero però difficilmente giustificato quel concetto limitato: Ringstones (1999), Mirror Of The Sea (2000), Front Row Centre (2000), Nightwalkers (2000), The View (2000), Visiting Star (2000), I Paint For Love Of Color (2001), Islands (2001), Nights (2001), Die Spiegelmanufaktur (2002), realizzato con Jim O'Rourke, Nights (2002), Solaris (2002), che introduceva elementi di musica d'avanguardia dissonante, A Pilgrim's Solace (2003), Figures In A Landscape (2004), Places Of Light (2004), Under The Sun (2004), Nightwalkers (2005) realizzato con Andreas Martin, Still Valley (2005) e il più denso Viking Burial For A French Car (2005).Goldfall (2006) è uno dei suoi lavori migliori, mentre l'inferiore Time Of Hayfield (2007) manipolava le note del pianoforte di Vikki Jackman. Vega (2006) proponeva invece un'atmosfera più eterea.The Days After (2007) raccoglie lavori di Mirror risalenti ai primissimi anni del nuovo millennio.Isolde, ovvero il duo di Andrew Chalk e Robin Barnes, pubblicarono All Things To Fall Like Marching (Penny Poppet, 2005), You're Alone In Red Riding Picture (2005) e On Waving And Drowning (Penny Poppet, 2006).The Cable House (Faraway Press, 2009) creava delicati spettri di melodie dalle note del pianoforte. Metà dell'album è occupato dai venti minuti di Naybuchi.In Flaxfleet Clouds Uplifted Autumn Gave Passage To Kind Nature (Faraway Press, 2009) documenta una collaborazione con Daisuke Suzuki (un ex collaboratore degli Ora).Ghost Of Nakhodka (2009 - Siren, 2010) era un viaggio nell'ambient e nella musica da camera minimalista.Violin By Night (Faraway Press, 2011) proponeva droni lirici ottenuti da pianoforte, chitarra, elettronica e vari field recording.Echoes Pastoraux (La Scie Doree, 2011), accreditato a Elodie, documenta una collaborazione tra Andrew Chalk e il compositore belga Timo Van Lujik. La Lumiere Parfumee (Faraway Press, 2012) era il suo seguito.Andrew Chalk lanciò il progetto Marsfield pubblicando The Towering Sky (Faraway Press, 2010), registrato con Vikki Jackman, Robin Barnes e Brendan Walls nel 2005, e Three Sunsets Over Marsfield (Faraway Press, 2010), contenente registrazioni risalenti al 2002.Forty-Nine Views In Rhapsodies' Wave Serene (Faraway Press, 2012) contains 49 delicate watercolors, pushing the chamber ambient music of Violins By Night, Ghost Of Nakhodka, and The Cable House to its minimal and melodic extreme, far removed from the droning monoliths that established his credentials.(Translation by/ Tradotto da xxx)Se sei interessato a tradurre questo testo, contattami

items.body: In 1989, Annea Lockwood released A Sound Map of the Hudson River, followed by A Sound Map of the Danube in 2008 and A Sound Map of the Housatonic River in 2013. Inspired by Lockwood, Brad Seippel (known here as thruoutin) traveled to Louisiana to record Tchefuncte Soundmap, tracing the course of the 70-mile river whose name honors a culture over two millennia old. Ironically, the generous (1 hour 44 minute) album begins not with the sound of obvious water, but with birdsong and distant traffic. The river is audible, but drowned out; later it will grow less shy. Seippel writes that he was first frustrated by the “imperfections” of human intrusion, but later came to regard them as honest reflections of the current biophony. Gators are present at the first location, though only their splashes are heard; the thought of gators cancels fantasies of drifting lazily down the river in an inner tube. By “Little Tchfuncte 2,” the human noise has grown ever more apparent. Few untouched places remain. Seippel wonders whether the beavers, egrets and other local residents have acclimated to the sounds of humanity, the listener wonders whether we have done so as well. Those who come to hear the river are likely enchanted by the natural sounds, such as the canopy of crickets in the next piece, while also being distracted by the unnatural sounds as they learn that “getting away from it all” seems no longer possible. There are exceptions: the joy of hearing children at play in “Bogue Falaya Park 1” and the soft, comforting clacks of “I-12 Bridge.” In “Bogue Falaya Park 2,” we finally hear the river – the main attraction! – flowing at full power. Much of the album become a pilgrimage, like a hidden image puzzle, as one yearns to hear such power again. One yearns to know how far from the river the recordist is traveling, or if the river is reduced to a trickle at various junctures. This also brings up the question, “What do we expect from nature?” Do we expect it to nourish us, or understand that we also need to nourish it in return? The rush to visit “unspoiled places,” thereby spoiling them, underlines the point. “Guste Island” is one of the shortest and most powerful pieces, as it highlights the wind, water and wildlife, all in concise fashion. “Barge 1” and “Barge 2” offer a quiet tribute to the intersection of humanity and nature; a local real estate company writes, “this premier community offers a serene retreat surrounded by nature while remaining just minutes from top-rated schools.” One can see the attraction, but also the problem. Finally Seippel arrives at the Tchefuncte River Lighthouse, a historic landmark built in 1837 that guards the shores of Lake Pontchartrain from a tiny peninsula. The river normally flows to the lake, save for times of intense flooding, when the flow is reversed. The album is bisected by an interview with Park Ranger Steve Poss, and ends with an interview with lifelong resident Dennis Bloom. If this were a double CD, one would expect that these would close each disc. Poss waxes rhapsodically about the limpkins and apple snails, who lay “bubble gum” eggs. He makes friends with rabbits and “communes” with an alligator. Bloom reminisces about boating trips on Lake Pontchartrain and camping by the river. The water laps beside his words, like a caring companion. “It’s just beautiful,” he says, “until the hurricane comes.” It’s a foreboding note to end on, making the listener question, “could we be the thousand-year storm?” For now, ol’ man river jes’ keeps rollin’ along. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Roots reggae singer Marcus Gad built his fifth album around the Kanak custom of his home island, New Caledonia, where communities share what the land provides. The title track “For All” puts that straight into its hook, changing a single word across one line: he chants “it a go shine for all” for the sun, then “it a go fall on all” for the rain. The sun and the rain reach everyone, and nobody owns either. The singe marks the first time Gad unites his distinct recording frameworks, combining the organic instrumentation of his live band Tribe with the electronic engineering of producer Tamal. Tribe lays down a slow, steady one-drop riddim guided by Franck Paulin‘s organ work and a full brass section, while Tamal handles the final mix and digital layers. Out on 19 June through Easy Star Records and Big Scoop Records,, For All is Gad’s first album in three years. items.body: Review by tszirmay — No beating around the bush, flaming or otherwise, ESP Project is one of my perennials, an ongoing love affair that began 11 years ago with the debut "Invisible Din" that had the luxury of having me fall head over heels (a la Tears for Fears!) with their style of melancholic /romantic prog , laden with sumptuous melodies and a solid rhythmic support (Hello Mark Brzezicki) . Multi-talented Tony Lowe certainly has a distinct style which he masters all along his nine follow up albums, each one a splendid reverie that garnered high critical praise, nothing overtly technical mind you, complex only in the genial manner it is all put together in terms of production (Tony has a long list of successful adventures in that department!). Suave lead vocalist Peter Coyle is back again for another microphone appointment, as well as the afore mentioned Brzezicki, a solid rhythmic propeller with impeccable credentials , to say the least. The cover art is always consistent with the musical message, colorful, elegant and expressive of the content within. Seven mid-sized tracks, each superbly constructed, all for our listening pleasure. The sensation of musical silk gliding over soft skin is immediately palpable on "Into Molecular", the shuffling tempo wasting little time in settling in, the glistening guitar adding to the hushed seduction as Peter initiates the tale. Dreamy keyboard-driven atmospherics weave an orchestral panacea, from which a delightful solo would emerge, the entire arrangement blooming into a myriad of articled colorations, soothing molecules of sound that show no hint of anger.The velvet touch comes across on "Time Slips Sideways", riding on a wave of melodic swoon that is hard to ignore, the flowing percussive pulse muscular, permitting access to some ear-pleasing candy. The various synthesized layers coalesce within a dense construct, the hovering electric guitar overflowing with a bright disposition can only elicit smiles of approval. The orchestral send-off is also unexpected and cinema worthy! The freshness stays very much intact on the ebullient "Imagination", a nearly 10-minute fluffy cloud of beautiful notes and chords, where Peter's carefree delivery becomes quite addictive, the vaporous instrumental stride washing away any trepidation as if 'time slipped sideways'! Tony is also unafraid to delve into superimposed variations that are bold and startling, such as inserting delicate percolating shifts, as well as letting both the organ and the synthesizers do some travelling. His bass work is never discreet, at certain moments even daring to take over the spotlight. This last comment is openly obvious on the throttling "A Beam of Light", a late-night cruise into more vivacious rhythms, the bass overdrive illuminating the highway ahead, the wind releasing love as the bass caresses the skin, the guitars clanging, the drums pounding. A roadside stop within the darkened horizon, gives the listener the opportunity to gaze up to the sky, and let the imagination run wild, "Random Stars" diverts the mind from the routine realities and frees up pent-up emotions, 'there is nothing to hide' anymore. The undeniable liberation that is the message of peace. Here specifically, one can detect a clear Beatles influence, as if ESP channeled the spirit of that legendary band into a modern version of the White Album (in my mind, the first progressive masterpiece in music). What else could possibly follow ? "Weightless" stretches the contrasts with a frothy symphonic melody, sublime in merging floating hymns with orchestral splendour, the surreal vocals oozing bluesy class and a stunning organ passage that rekindles fond memories of whiter shades of pale. Crown that with backing vocal effects and a long and delirious axe solo and this becomes a masterclass piece that yearns for applause. The second longest track "The Feedback and the Fire" switches into less dreamy vocals, the singing more forceful and intense, the tempo astonishingly athletic, amid a kaleidoscope of intricate layers of keyboards running the show, while the bass pants all along the watchtower, unbothered. Lose yourself in the subtle spell of letting your mind perceive the senses, eyes closed for there is way more colour in your brain that anything you may ever see. A sure-fire certainty when stimulated by such a wide variety of gorgeous sounds. This is the definition of healing. The brazen and bustling finale reminds us that mellowness can have even more depth that one may think. If you haven't yet plunged into the ESP spell, too bad for you, as you are missing out on a level of consistent quality that escapes the usual traps that arbitrary dismissals may cause. Mature, fiery, secure and exalting music that you may just fall in love with. I know I did , way back when. 5 ultra fleshly assessments

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Rick is back with his 21st album, which is the 14th in succession which I have reviewed, starting all the way back with 2009's 'Falling Through Rainbows'. These days Rick is hugely consistent with his output, with this being is seventh album in seven years, and with exactly the same personnel as last year's 'Perspective', three of whom have been with him for more than 20 years. Heavily influenced by The Moody Blues and the more atmospheric releases from David Gilmour and Steve Hackett, one always knows what one is going to get with Miller, a heavily dreamy version of symphonic rock with his vocals providing another ambient nature.Mind you, those who think he has forgotten what the volume control is for on his guitar, or the use of dynamics, should look closely at the longest track on the album, "The Game". It is this song which has been used as the inspiration for the cover art, and changes melody and approach during its nine plus minutes. I always smile when a new Miller album is presented to me, as I know I am always going to enjoy it and the only decision I have to make is whether it is going to be five stars or merely four, as over the last fifteen years or so I have never awarded anything less, which is highly unusual for me. For some strange reason Miller has never really been recognised in the higher echelons of the underground scene, but that is never due to lack of wonderful material. Those of us in the know have been raving about him for years, and hopefully we will long continue to do so as his highly constructed, polished and refined style of progressive rock is always a joy from beginning to end.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — With David Sinclair back on keyboards for Caravan, the band recaptured some of its lost essence; while the funk and jazz leanings of Waterloo Lily had been welcome, For Girls Who Grow Plump in the Night saw them reclaim certain elements, such as a specific harmonic lyricism and a rock-and-roll spirit, alongside a sound defined by the viola, a new facet already evident in "Memory Lain, Hugh / Headloss.""Hoedown" links them to the Welsh band Man, who also dabbled in country rock, but things get interesting again on "C'thlu Thlu," where the sound darkens to the point of incorporating scales reminiscent of King Crimson, alongside a keyboard part that starts out funky and stretches to fill the rest of the track."The Dog, the Dog, He's at It Again" is a new classic for the band; they will perform it live many times, and each rendition will be unique. Here, the sound of the viola is truly integrated into Caravan's natural composition. Masterfully sung by Pye Hastings, the track builds until the instrumental section, featuring keyboards, guitar, and bass, washes over everything, culminating in the entry of the viola, which draws upon elements reminiscent of Rick Wakeman and the Electric Light Orchestra."Be Alright / Chance of a Lifetime" continues in a rock vein, driven by prominent guitar work, with Pye Hastings almost channeling Steve Howe as he hits those soaring high notes, while the song's second half recaptures Caravan's signature mellow essence; the psychedelic keyboard solos of the early days are replaced here by journeys led by the violin, though distinct from Jean-Luc Ponty's style, serving the song rather than acting as a centerpiece.L'auberge du Sanglier showcases the very best facets of Caravan, the orchestral, the subtle, and the rock-oriented. The New Symphonia Orchestra, with whom the band would record their next studio album, collaborates here; the guitar and strings blend beautifully, managing to sound surprisingly raw at times. David Sinclair's piano section, set against the strings and then joined by the woodwinds, possesses such delicacy that it adds extra value to the album; when the Minimoog enters the mix alongside the orchestra, the piece stands out as the album's finest (even though my heart belongs to "The Dog, the Dog, He's at It Again!"). Then, as the orchestra swells in volume, accompanied by the drums, the keyboard improvises, darting into every corner of the composition like a bouncing laser beam, reminiscent of George Martin's orchestrations for Jeff Beck's Blow by Blow.

While in structure and overall effect similar to their 2024 full length debut, they are sounding more British isles and less scattershot Euro than before. Not to say this is any more original, what with JETHRO TULL comparisons likely to plague them forever, even though their commitment to being a Celtic rock band first and foremost is far more convincing than Ian Anderson's preference for diversification. This places them closer top the likes of a more patriarchal STEELEYE SPAN or even RUNRIG or OYSTERBAND territory. They do sing one track in Welsh which, combined with the GPS references of "Lakesongs of Elbid", belies possible ethnic origins. Perhaps not as prog or as wide ranging, it's also more consistent, hence making that final character in the title a welcome hint of the springboarding future.
