items.body: Review by tszirmay — The Sheffield arranger, composer and multi-instrumentalist rises once again, landing straight to the top of the Symphonic prog pedestal with another outstanding release that merits the attention of all prog fans, his sixth venture that includes last year's 20th anniversary remake of his debut 2005 album "All in the Golden Afternoon". While all his records are of exceptional quality, as well as highly rated within the community, as he maintains a stylistic standard that is purely his own, this new opus might just conquer the prog Everest once and for all. So, when we talk about symphonic Prog , the two words are of maximal importance , as the balancing act required to blend the two together in harmonious deliverance is a challenging task. Arranging classical music, especially keyboard-based material is a bold enterprise, as the numerous prog legends of the glory years of the 70s stamped the rock element for eternity (we know who they are). Credibility, originality as well as respect of tradition are all required elements. Ian handles this arduous task by fully understanding how this brand of music needs to be listened to. The audience yearns for an immersive experience, with a time, a place and a story to plunge into with full engagement, in order to savor all the detailed components and how it will affect the pleasure nodes. From the three-part opening suite "How Dreams Do Creep (for Souls Asleep), to the sprawling "Leonardo" with its five acts , the casual listener is instantly drawn into abandoning any background music pretense, dropping all the multi-tasking maladies of our times , and just close the eyes, and let the imagination roam freely. That my friends is what music should be about: liberation. Ian wastes no time in establishing the foundational platform on which he will develop his craft on the opener, lessons learned from past innovators like early Genesis, including Ant Phillips (Slow Dance era) , as the delicate interface between the mellotron symphonics, the pastoral elements so dear to the British folk-rock tradition (The Strawbs, Gryphon, Magicfolk, Iona, etc?), and a brawny bass governance leaps forward throughout. Lather on some heady keyboards, both organ, piano, and synths, toss in some slicing guitar shavings and some serious syncopation on the percussive side, and you are immediately plunged into an alternate fantasy world of your own making. As if to further the point, "Late States , Eden's Gates" eliminates any possible argument that lethargic arrangements could rule the roost, quite to the contrary, the pace is throbbing, expansive, and at times, breathtakingly bold. That stodgy bass is such a devourer of emotions, egging on the remaining instrumental deliberations. A moment of reflection on the short "Enitharmon's Dream" wanders into dreamier territory yet still packs quite the wallop when challenged, very indicative of the album cover's intuitive message. The epic, nearly 13 minute "Cretan Angel" elects a mythological revisit of the Greek classics, your choice of Iliad or the Odyssey, a vocal and acoustic main frame on which to establish presence, a light passing through the veil of illusion, and a state of temporary silence. The progression is effortless, a gradual build-up of symphonic festivity, where details vie with overall impact for the attentive ear. The second half raises the temperature with stormier motifs, booming drums ushering in grandiose walls of synthesized orchestrations, and an expertly sculpted guitar solo that seek to rival the electronic keyboard arsenal, both putting up quite the fuss. The swirling finale is rightfully over the top. A duo of 5-minute pieces are next up, with "Fresco" surging into more delicate territory , a warm synth weaving between tick-tock drums, a massive synth-bass echoing throughout the musical cupola, craning necks desperate for focusing on the intricate details. The electric guitar solo overtly takes this straight into the celestial heavens, with a sprawling Gilmour-esque burst that screeches emphatically. Sublime. Another bucolic, flute-led orchestral romp on "Of Aether, Rose and Spangling Dew", the soaring harmonic chants a pure delicacy, church organ lagging close behind, cherubs looking down and smiling, establishing a comfortable numbness from which no one wishes to escape. Gloriously intense. The 11 and a quarter finale is the absolute highpoint, an exquisite exercise in cutting-edge, soundtrack-worthy cinematographic immersion. The stylishness of the piano, in tandem with its bass guitar counterpart, the eloquent choral voices, the euphoric cymbals crashing undeterred, as the melodic accrual marches onward and upward, is wholly phenomenal. The hushed lead vocals appear to express more than reverence, as the crescendo is ultimately attained and the whistling winds scatter the leaves of memories past. The evolution maintains nevertheless a continuity that keeps the focus on the overall canvas, adding a plethora of detail, power and insistence that was deliberately arranged to achieve a haunting apotheosis, perhaps even apocalyptic irrevocability. Symphonic Prog has a new classic to enjoy for ever more. Whatever your preferences are and how they may influence your choices, there is a time and a place for this style of escape within our over stimulated, at times helter-skelter (rarely has a Beatles title been more applicable to our current mayhem), and many would be negligent at their own peril of not checking out this gemlike flame! This release needs to be both heard and felt. 4.5 glittering emeralds

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — From its humble origins as Wiccan Rede to its earliest albums as NEGURA BUNGET, this Romanian bandelegantly began weaving in an increasingly strong aspect of progressive rock with each releaseslowly emerging as something more complex than what preceded. Two albums in and NEGURA BUNGET was amajor world class powerhouse of exquisitely designed atmospheric Pagan metal that took fulladvantage of the progressive metal lexicon and with N CRUGU BRADULUI, the band's third full-lengthrelease, the band that now consisted of the original duo drummer Negru and guitarist / vocalist /keyboardist Hupogrammos Disciple's along with guitarist Cristian Popescu "Sol Faur" and guestbassist Ursu went for the progressive jugular.Wild claims state that the title translates into something exotic such as "Through The Deepness OfThe Fir Tree Heights," which is parroted across the internet but it seems that the album's title NCRUGU BRADULU simply translates as "Around The Fir Tree." The album debuted the band's fullestprogressive potentials which features an epic concept of the natural cycle of the universe andbroken down into four lengthy tracks that each represents one of the four seasons with tracksranging between 12 and 15 minutes in length. The album ramps up the band's flawless atmosphericfusion of aggressive black metal along with synthesized arrangements and eerie ambient effects.Likewise the band introduced more aspects of its native Romanian folk music with the timeless soundsof Transylvania seeping in.With four chapters simply titled "I" through "IV," N CRUGU BRADULUI offers haunting atmosphericbuildup to ratchet up the mystique before erupting into a frenzy of black metal bombast and in theprocess evokes the dreamy atmospheric ambience of Burzum with the high octane energetic drive ofDarkthrone only fueled with the folk flavors of its homeland. "I" takes opens elegantly with a post-rock inspired introduction that slowly ratchets up the tension to a wonderful display of exquisitemusicianship in cahoots with well crafted compositions that keep your attention focused and thennever let you off the hook for the album's near 54 minute journey. The album elegantly blends thePagan mystique of Romanian antiquity while capturing the dark essence of Transylvania's #1 export,the Dracula mythos despite that not being the subject.While the following "OM" gets touted as the band's masterpiece of its career and for great reason asit takes what was presented on N CRUGU BRADULUI to even greater levels of ingenuity andexperimentation, for my tastes i find this predecessor to be on equal standing of its more laudedcounterpart. This album is flawless in execution and showcases the band's first perfecting balancebetween the atmospheric cryptic nature of the album's thematic structuring and magnificently matureblack metal that seamlessly fuses in the Romanian folk musical touches. The band had matured in everpossible way and although "OM" may be a tad more diverse with more excursions into pure folkritualistic effects, N CRUGU BRADULUI evokes the true majesty of Romanian black metal at its toptier level and every bit as enthralling as its followup. Just as much as a classic.

Of all of their 80s releases, this is the album that embraces mostthoroughly the neo-medieval, tribal-like aesthetic and at this point their project bears almost noresemblance to the earlier darkwave post-punk sound (as heard on their self-titled debut LP or on'Spleen and Ideal', for example). At the same time, 'The Serpent's Egg' exhibits an immaculate tastefor atmospheric ambient sounds, which comes through in spades on the more vocal-dominated tracks.This record definitely evokes a feeling of awe and splendor, almost as if you are listening to thesoundtrack of a surreal dream, and one can easily understand how much medieval folk music hadinfluenced the Australian duo's taste, whose infatuation with the spiritual side of music here isboth daring and earnest. And while it is incredibly difficult to highlight certain tracks on analbum like this one, some of the mesmerizing compositions appearing on 'The Serpent's Egg' includethe phenomenal opener 'The Host of Seraphim', the song 'Severance', which is one of the few songs onthis record featuring the vocals of Perry, the majestic 'In the Kingdom of the Blind the One-EyedAre Kings' as well as 'Mother Tongue' and 'Ullyses' - all of these tracks have some magical qualityto them that only Dead Can Dance are capable of birthing, which is very likely why 'The Serpent'sEgg' continues to be one of their most praised and valued releases. Delightful and delirious, thisrecord defies genre and explores music as a majestic living organism.

It is Ozrics mixed with Hawkwind with dashes of �resund Space Collective thrown in for good measure, but always direct and as much at home at a rave as it is between your ears when played on headphones (always at a decent volume). items.body: Review by kev rowland — Unless you have been under a rock somewhere you will know that Rush are not the only Canadians making an unexpected comeback in 2026, as the original line-up of Mike Levine (bass, keyboards, synthesizer, piano, backing vocals), Gil Moore (drums, percussion, lead and backing vocals and Rik Emmett (guitar, lead and backing vocals, synthesizer, keyboards, bass) are also hitting the road. Of course there will always be a record label tie-in, and as there is no new product to release, we instead have another compilation of their greatest hits (many of which are single edits). I have all the albums featuring the original guys, having first discovered them when they released the single "Hold On" which soon led me to buying their third album, 1979's 'Just A Game'. Their technical melodic hard rock was a style I really enjoyed, a long way from the NWOBHM scene I was experiencing as a teenager in the UK, and playing this album now is like visiting old friends.Every song contained on this 10-track set was a hit single in Canada or America, but I was somewhat surprised to see that "I Live For The Weekend" was missing as that has always been one of my favourites (I have it as a 12" single) but then realised that for some weird reason it was only a hit in the UK. But given it was the only song of theirs to ever chart there it would have been nice to see it, but I guess Americans/Canadians may not see it that way. This is a great introduction to one of Canada's greatest ever hard rock exports, and while their return may been overshadowed somewhat, there is no doubt they are worthy inductees to the Canadian Music Industry Hall of Fame, the Canadian Music Hall of Fame, and Canada's Walk of Fame, even if there has been no new studio album since 1992. "Lay It On The Line", "Hold On", "Magic Power", "I Can Survive" are all here, ans in many ways this is a solid release.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Protos was formed in 1977 by Rory Ridley-Duff (keyboards) and Steve Anscombe (guitars), and their 1982 debut album, 'One Day a New Horizon', had an expanded line-up which included Neil Goldsmith, Iain Carnegie and Nigel Rippon. By 1984 the band was no more, but Ridley-Duff and Anscombe stayed active in the music scene, and following on from a CD reissue of the album in 2006 they released a new album the following year. What we have here is a new keyboards and drums version of the original with Ridley-Duff being joined by drummer Alex Warwick. Apparently Anscombe was involved in the arrangements but was too ill to be musically active as he was suffering from a terminal illness, and on the front cover it states, "In memory of Stephen Anscombe".It is somewhat unusual for a band to revisit their debut so long after the original was released, and although I probably know more underground prog than many, I must confess I have never come across the original. This album has the same six songs but not knowing the debut I cannot comment on just how different it is. What did surprise me however is just how much I kept thinking of Soniq Theater while I was playing this, and I was somewhat surprised to see it wasn't Alfred when I looked to see what the album was. However, the use of "real" drums makes a significant difference and definitely adds to the polish on this release. It is not surprising to discover this is a remake of a much older album as it still has plenty of Eighties' feel about it, probably aided by the keyboard sounds being utilised. It is an interesting release as opposed to essential, and in some ways appears to have been influenced by Steve Hackett and Anthony Phillips' pastoral works, which is something of a weird thing to say given they are both guitarists and this is keyboards, but my mind works in weird and wonderful ways. It is a pleasant enough progressive romp, and I am sure anyone who has enjoyed the original release will want to seek this out.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Poly-Math are a British instrumental act formed in 2013 by guitarist Tim Walters who was originally drummer of post-rock band Monsters Build Mean Robots. He wanted to focus on guitar and instrumental music and was soon joined by bassist Joe Branton and drummer Chris Woollison. Shortly after the release of their 2018 album, 'House Of Wisdom | We Are The Devil' they were joined by American multi-instrumentalist Josh Geesner, who had relocated to the UK, and although they moved to a quintet for a short while with saxophonist Chris Olsen joining the ranks they are once again operating as a quartet. Musically this is all over the place with an incredibly diverse set of influences ranging from early classic prog, Ethio-jazz, post-rock, math rock, African tribal rhythms and so much more. There is a great deal going on at all times with hugely complex and complicated arrangements and massive note density, which means the listener needs to pay close attention to what is taking place or running the very real risk of missing out. Everyone involved is a master musician, yet there is little in the way of egos or hogging the limelight as all have a hugely important part to play in the overall sound as the percussion can be working in one direction which is totally at odds with the guitar while the bass is off on its own melody and the keyboards are taking another route, yet when they combine, it all makes sense. They will converge at a point; take a split second to remind each other they are all in the same band and then they are off again!While math rock is the main style, they bring in a great deal more, and Woollison is a true percussionist, not just a drummer wanting to expand his resume, which adds greatly to the overall impact.Truly progressive, this is a fascinating album from beginning to end.

items.body: Une Vraie Gothique (translated as A True Goth) is a French duo formed by Ulrika and Ferdinand Legendre. “R.D.V. Au Cimetière” is their debut album, and it immediately caught the attention of Manic Depression Records. The project’s name may sound unmistakably Gothic, but the musical influences stem from a much broader palette. This is primarily an Electro album, blending elements of Electro-Wave, EBM, Techno, and a subtle Gothic atmosphere into a highly danceable whole. The lyrics possess a poetic quality, occasionally veering into the humorous and sometimes even the provocative. The songs are performed in French by the male vocalist and in German by the female vocalist. The interplay between these two voices is one of the album’s greatest strengths, often creating the impression of an ongoing dialogue. The overall production occasionally reminds me of Grausame Töchter, albeit with far less emphasis on sexuality and provocation. Personally, I am most drawn to the more powerful tracks driven by a strong EBM bassline, but nearly every song offers something worthwhile. For me, “R.D.V. Au Cimetière” is an exciting and refreshing debut. Une Vraie Gothique is undoubtedly a band that deserves to be discovered, and they clearly possess the talent and originality needed to reach a much wider audience in the future. (Rating:8½). items.body: Calva Y Nada, the German electro and dark-wave project of Constantin Warter, release the live album “El calor de Zwickau” on October 2, 2026 through emmobiz Records. The label issues the Club Seilerstraße, Zwickau recording across vinyl and CD editions. Calva Y Nada bring a German electro and dark wave that mixes EBM rhythms and minimal-electronic textures with German- and Spanish-language vocals. The “El calor de Zwickau” set runs fifteen tracks, among them “Die Reise,” “Aufprall,” “Schmerzenskrone,” “Dias Felices,” “Habemus Papam,” “Fernes Leid,” “La pura mierda” and “Der Sturm,” closing with an encore of “Borriquito,” “Paradies” and “Rascheln.” Calva Y Nada ‘El calor de Zwickau’ editions emmobiz Records releases “El calor de Zwickau” on October 2, 2026 in several editions, including a double LP, an LP set, an LP box, a CD set, a CD box and a three-CD edition. Part of the run includes a bonus 7-inch or 3-inch CD with a one-off joint performance of “Deutschland” by Prager Handgriff and Calva Y Nada. The three-CD edition pairs the new “El calor de Zwickau” recording with the earlier “Live @ Club Seilerstraße” set and an encore disc. Side-Line covered the project’s 2024 “Live @ Club Seilerstraße Zwickau” release and the 2026 “La Pura Mierda” EP. About Calva Y Nada Calva Y Nada is the German electro and dark-wave project founded in 1990 by Constantin Warter, who records under the name Breñal. The project grew out of his earlier group Glatze des Willens — “Calva” is Spanish for the German word “Glatze” (bald). Calva Y Nada released early albums on Hyperium, including “Dias Felizes” (1991) and “Monologe eines Baumes” (1993), followed by “¡Palpita, Corazón, Palpita!” (1994) and a final studio album, “Schlaf,” in 1998. The project went quiet at the end of the 1990s and returned in the 2010s and 2020s. Since 2024, emmobiz Records has run a vinyl reissue and live program for the catalogue, and the 2026 EP “La Pura Mierda” marked its first new studio material since 1998. “El calor de Zwickau” continues that run with a live document released on October 2, 2026.

items.body: Boy Harsher returns with “Jeans,” their first new original song under the Boy Harsher banner since the cinematic 2022 stretch that brought The Runner and “Burn It Down” from the Halloween Ends soundtrack into their dance-noir universe. Arriving after the announcement of The Heartbreak Tour, the new track feels less like a simple comeback than a bold re-entry: a stonewashed post-punk fever dream about escape, ambition, image, and the uneasy moment when the fantasy of freedom gets refitted into a commodity. Musically, “Jeans” may be Boy Harsher’s most openly post-punk-sounding track yet. More guitar-forward than anything in their catalog, and with a bubbling synth beat, it finds Gus Muller riding a bouncy guitar riff that sounds as if it were pilfered from his foray into Safe Mind. It is a bold breath of fresh air for the duo, cutting through their usual synth-driven machinery with a wiry melodic lift. Threaded beneath it is a steel-slide guitar, giving the song the perfect western cowboy twang to match the line-dancing imagery in the video. The juxtaposition works because Jae Matthews knows exactly how to occupy the space around it. Her vocal here is sultry, cool, and lightly scuffed at the edges, less an incantation from a dark room than a sideways glance from the passenger seat. Against the guitar’s buoyant post-punk snap, “Jeans” takes on an almost Pretenders-like shape: sleek, restless, and deceptively direct, with noir atmosphere refracted through something closer to a new wave song’s 80s pop pulse. In a statement accompanying the release, Matthews says: “‘Jeans’ came from two distinct experiences between Gus and I. I was living in a ‘small town,’ trying to understand my life and attempting to find freedom from the pressure of being ‘anyone.’ Meanwhile, Gus was chasing his aspirations in the Big Apple. We were both seeking our dreams in polar ways … and in this cheeky way, ‘Jeans’ speaks on that quest through our commodification of a dream.” The band also described the video’s concept on Instagram: “We wanted to make our own Robert Palmer, “Addicted to Love.” We wanted to line dance in latex. Hot hands and cattle prods. We wanted to try to encapsulate that small-town feeling in an inaccessible apple.” Filmed by Owen Smith-Clark and edited by Chris Campion, the Boy Harsher-directed video places a pink-haired The 7th Girl, Ella, in a large, mostly empty room with fluorescent lights, tall windows, and pale walls. A group of dancers in black latex enters and performs line-dance choreography around her. Matthews sings in the room while Muller plays guitar, and both appear on old television monitors throughout the clip. The video cuts between close-ups of boots, gloves, latex, denim, faces, and the dancers’ formations. Some shots show the performers carrying cattle-prod-like props; others focus on the pink-haired woman as she watches the group, moves with them, and appears against a warm, western-colored backdrop. The clip keeps returning to the monitors, where close-ups of eyes and performance footage flicker inside the frame. A small town can feel like a sealed room; yet ambition can feel like another kind of enclosure. Freedom looks different from far away, especially when someone has already figured out how to turn longing into a look. Whether “Jeans” is the first flare from a larger body of work or simply the opening signal of Boy Harsher’s next phase, it arrives with the uneasy precision of a transmission from somewhere familiar and wonderfully strange. Watch the video for “Jeans” below: “Jeans” lands as Boy Harsher prepares for The Heartbreak Tour, their first extensive North American headlining run since the 2022 tour cycle around The Runner, when select dates paired the live show with screenings of the duo’s short horror film. They have continued to surface through select shows, festival appearances, remix work, soundtrack projects, and adjacent solo endeavors, but the center of gravity has shifted away from the usual album-tour pattern and toward film, scoring, and world-building. Matthews and Muller, who met in Savannah while studying film, first released Lesser Man as a small-run cassette before the EP became an underground hit. They followed with Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016 and Careful in 2019, sharpening their cold, body-moving electronics into something increasingly cinematic. That impulse became explicit with The Runner, the duo’s 2022 short horror film and accompanying soundtrack, written, produced, and directed by Matthews and Muller. The project blurred album, score, and visual world-building, pairing the duo’s darker instrumentals with guest turns from Mariana Saldaña of BOAN on “Machina” and Cooper B. Handy, aka Lucy, on “Autonomy.” The Machina thread continued in 2024 with the Machina EP, which expanded the track with alternate versions and remixes. Boy Harsher also kept a steady presence through remix work, including their 2024 rework of Pet Shop Boys’ “New London Boy,” a pairing that made sense: two duos fascinated by desire, distance, pop architecture, and the strange glamour of the city after dark. Matthews, meanwhile, has been building a parallel life in film and solo-adjacent work. She wrote My Animal, the Jacqueline Castel-directed horror romance starring Bobbi Salvör Menuez and Amandla Stenberg, which premiered at the 2023 Sundance Film Festival. This year, she stepped out under her own name with a cover of Buzz Kull’s “Man On The Beat,” released digitally March 20 and issued as a limited 12-inch through Heartworm Press on April 17. The physical edition, released as Heartworm #140 in an edition of 500, pairs Matthews’ version with a Spike Hellis remix on the B-side. Muller has continued to deepen his own work as a composer and producer. His score for My Animal, released by Sacred Bones, marked his debut feature film score and was written and recorded at his home studio in Northampton using hardware and analog synthesizers. He has also pursued Safe Mind, his collaborative project with Cooper B. Handy. The duo’s debut album, Cutting the Stone, arrived in 2025 through Nude Club, extending the chemistry first heard when Handy appeared on Boy Harsher’s The Runner soundtrack. The biggest new chapter, however, is The Lonely Woman, Boy Harsher’s first feature film as directors. Written and directed by Matthews and Muller, the rural New England horror-thriller stars Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, Sturgill Simpson, Will Oldham, and Jake Weary, with Boy Harsher also providing the score. The Heartbreak Tour began with a June 26 appearance at 1015 Folsom in San Francisco before properly kicking into gear Sept. 25 at Basilica Hudson in Hudson, New York. From there, Boy Harsher will move through Boston, Montreal, Toronto, Detroit, Chicago, Minneapolis, Denver, Portland, Seattle, Vancouver, Oakland, Los Angeles, Del Mar, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Fort Worth, New Orleans, Atlanta, Asheville, Washington, D.C., Philadelphia, and Queens, where the tour wraps Nov. 5 at Knockdown Center. The routing includes two-night stands at Chicago’s Metro, Portland’s Revolution Hall, and Seattle’s The Showbox, along with an Oct. 24 appearance at Sick New World – DFW in Fort Worth. Support on select dates includes Choir Boy, Evanora Unlimited, True Blue, and Kassie Krut. The centerpiece of the fall trek lands on Halloween night, when Boy Harsher headline Making Time Pure Halloween at Franklin Music Hall in Philadelphia. The Oct. 31 All Hallows’ Eve event also features Model/Actriz live, Conducta, Marie Davidson on DJ duty, Kassie Krut live, and Dave P., plus a futuristic visual experience from Klip Collective.
